title: What is a shadow deployment, and how do you implement it?
shortTitle: What a shadow deployment is and how to implement it

s1_definition.profdef: A shadow deployment, also called traffic mirroring or dark launch, runs a new version of a service alongside the current one and sends it a copy of real production traffic without ever returning its responses to clients. The live version continues to serve every real response; the shadow version silently processes the mirrored requests so you can compare its behavior, performance, and correctness against the live one under genuine production load, with zero risk to users. Crucially, the shadow's side effects, like writing to databases or calling payment rails, must be isolated so mirrored traffic cannot cause real-world actions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India is training a new loan officer. Instead of letting the trainee approve real loans, the bank quietly hands the trainee a photocopy of every real application that the experienced officer is handling. The trainee works through each one and writes down what they would decide, but their decisions are never acted upon; only the experienced officer's real decisions affect customers. Later, the manager compares the trainee's answers against the real ones to see if the trainee is ready. The trainee is the shadow version, the photocopies are mirrored traffic, and the rule that the trainee's decisions never touch real accounts is the side-effect isolation.
s1_definition.oneliner: A shadow deployment mirrors a copy of real traffic to a new version whose responses are discarded and whose side effects are isolated, so you can validate it under true production load with zero user risk.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A shadow deployment, also called traffic mirroring or dark launch, runs a new version of a service alongside the current one and sends it a copy of real production traffic without ever returning its responses to clients. The live version continues to serve every real response; the shadow version silently processes the mirrored requests so you can compare its behavior, performance, and correctness against the live one under genuine production load, with zero risk to users. Crucially, the shadow's side effects, like writing to databases or calling payment rails, must be isolated so mirrored traffic cannot cause real-world actions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India is training a new loan officer. Instead of letting the trainee approve real loans, the bank quietly hands the trainee a photocopy of every real application that the experienced officer is handling. The trainee works through each one and writes down what they would decide, but their decisions are never acted upon; only the experienced officer's real decisions affect customers. Later, the manager compares the trainee's answers against the real ones to see if the trainee is ready. The trainee is the shadow version, the photocopies are mirrored traffic, and the rule that the trainee's decisions never touch real accounts is the side-effect isolation.

**One line to remember:** A shadow deployment mirrors a copy of real traffic to a new version whose responses are discarded and whose side effects are isolated, so you can validate it under true production load with zero user risk.

sections.s2_technical:
The core mechanism is traffic mirroring at a routing layer, usually the gateway or a service mesh. For each incoming request, the layer forwards it to the live service as normal and also sends a duplicate to the shadow service. The client only ever sees the live service's response; the shadow's response is read and discarded, or captured for comparison, but never returned.

The purpose is realistic validation. Synthetic tests and staging environments never fully reproduce production traffic patterns, odd inputs, and load. Shadowing lets the new version face exactly the real distribution of requests, so you catch performance regressions, memory issues, and subtle behavioral differences before the new version ever serves a real user. It is especially valuable for risky rewrites, where you want proof the new version matches the old under real conditions.

The single most important concern is side-effect isolation, and it is where shadow deployments go wrong. If the shadow service shares the live database and writes to it, the mirrored traffic will double-write records; if it calls the real payment rail, it will move real money twice. So the shadow must be pointed at an isolated or read-only datastore, use sandboxed or mocked versions of external systems, and never emit real notifications. A mirrored transfer must never actually move money. In banking this isolation is non-negotiable.

Response comparison is how you extract value. You capture the live and shadow responses for the same request and compare them, often asynchronously and offline, flagging mismatches in status, body, or timing. This comparison, sometimes called traffic diffing, tells you whether the new version is behaving equivalently. You also compare resource usage and latency, because a correct but slow new version is still a problem.

Implementation options vary by platform. In a service mesh like Istio, mirroring is a first-class feature: a VirtualService can specify a mirror destination and even a mirror percentage, so you mirror, say, ten percent of traffic. In Spring Cloud Gateway, you implement a filter that, after dispatching to the primary route, asynchronously fires a duplicate request to the shadow using a non-blocking client and ignores the result. At the load-balancer or proxy level, tools like Nginx or Envoy support request mirroring directly.

A senior nuance is cost and blast radius. Mirroring doubles the load on the mirrored path, so you often mirror only a sampled percentage and you ensure the mirror is fire-and-forget so a slow shadow never delays the real response. Another nuance is data sensitivity, because mirrored requests carry real customer data into the shadow environment, which must therefore meet the same security and compliance controls as production. A final nuance is distinguishing shadow from canary: a canary serves real responses to a small slice of users and so carries real risk, whereas a shadow serves no responses and carries essentially no user risk, which makes shadowing the safer first step before a canary.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has rewritten its interest-calculation service and must be certain the new version produces identical results to the old one before trusting it with real customers. Staging tests passed, but the team wants proof against real production requests, including the weird edge cases real customers generate. A shadow deployment lets the new version process real mirrored requests while the trusted old version keeps serving customers.

Problem 2 — The interest service writes computed interest to a ledger and sends notifications. If the shadow version shares those, mirrored traffic would double-post interest and double-notify customers. So the shadow must write to an isolated ledger and must not send real notifications.

The connection to the fix: we will build a mirroring gateway that sends each request to the live service and a copy to the shadow service, returns only the live response, and compares the two asynchronously, flagging mismatches. The shadow is wired to an isolated ledger and a no-op notifier so it has no real side effects.

What the code will do. There is an `InterestRequest` and an `InterestResponse`. There is a live `InterestServiceV1` and a shadow `InterestServiceV2`, each computing interest, where V2 has a deliberate subtle bug on one input to show the comparison catching it. The shadow uses an `IsolatedLedger` and a `NoOpNotifier`. There is a `TrafficDiffer` that records mismatches. There is a `MirroringGateway` that dispatches to live, mirrors fire-and-forget to shadow, compares, and returns only the live response. The demo sends several requests and prints which matched and which the differ flagged.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the plain-Java shadow demo
javac ShadowDemo.java
java com.bank.gateway.demo.ShadowDemo

# Istio traffic mirroring (real platform)
# VirtualService: http.route to v1 (100%), mirror to v2, mirrorPercentage 100
kubectl apply -f interest-virtualservice-mirror.yaml

# Spring Cloud Gateway shadow filter
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/shadow-deploy-gateway-1.0.0.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is four interest-calculation requests, including one with a zero principal that will expose a bug in the shadow version.

Step 1. The first request for Rajesh's account arrives. The gateway calls the live V1, which computes the interest correctly and returns it; this is the response the client receives. The gateway then fires a fire-and-forget copy to the shadow V2 and immediately returns the live response without waiting.

Step 2. Asynchronously, the shadow V2 processes the mirrored request. It computes the same interest, writes it to the isolated ledger, and calls the no-op notifier, so no real posting and no real notification happen. The differ compares V1's and V2's responses, they match, and a match is recorded.

Step 3. The second request for Priya is handled the same way. Live returns the real response to the client; shadow computes in the background with isolated side effects; the differ records another match. So far the new version looks equivalent.

Step 4. The third request has a zero principal. Live V1 correctly computes zero interest and returns it to the client. The shadow V2, which has a deliberate bug on zero principal, computes one rupee instead. The differ compares the two, sees they disagree, and flags a mismatch. This is exactly the kind of real-world edge case that staging might miss but production traffic reveals, caught here with zero impact on the customer, who still received the correct live answer.

Step 5. The fourth request matches again. The final report shows three matches and one mismatch. The team now has concrete evidence from real traffic that V2 is almost right but has a zero-principal bug to fix before it can be trusted, and no customer was ever affected and no real money or notification was ever touched by the shadow.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A shadow deployment, sometimes called traffic mirroring or a dark launch, runs a new version of a service next to the current one and sends it a copy of real production traffic, but its responses are never returned to clients. The live version keeps serving every real response, and the shadow version silently processes the mirrored requests so I can see how it behaves under genuine production load, with real inputs and real volume, before it ever serves a customer. The value is that staging and synthetic tests never fully reproduce production, so shadowing is how I get real proof that a new version is correct and fast enough.

The single most important rule, and the thing I always emphasize, is side-effect isolation. If the shadow version shares the live database or calls the real payment rail, the mirrored traffic will double-write records or move real money twice. So the shadow is pointed at an isolated or read-only datastore, uses sandboxed or mocked external systems, and never sends real notifications. In my banking work at National Bank of India, we shadow-tested a rewritten interest-calculation service exactly this way: the live version served customers and wrote the real ledger, while the shadow computed against an isolated ledger and a no-op notifier, so a mirrored interest calculation could never post real interest or alert a customer.

The way I extract value is response comparison, or traffic diffing. For each request I capture the live and shadow responses and compare them asynchronously, flagging any mismatch in status, body, or timing. In our interest rewrite, this is precisely how we caught a subtle bug: on a zero-principal account, the live version correctly returned zero while the new version returned one rupee. The customer still got the correct live answer, so there was zero impact, but we now had concrete evidence from real traffic that the new version had an edge-case bug to fix before we could trust it.

On implementation, a service mesh like Istio supports mirroring as a first-class feature, where a VirtualService names a mirror destination and even a mirror percentage; in Spring Cloud Gateway I implement a filter that, after dispatching to the live route, asynchronously fires a duplicate to the shadow and ignores the result. The nuances I always raise are cost, data sensitivity, and the contrast with canary. Mirroring doubles the load on that path and must be fire-and-forget so a slow shadow never delays the real response, which is why I often mirror only a sampled percentage. The mirrored requests carry real customer data into the shadow environment, so that environment must meet the same security and compliance controls as production. And I distinguish shadow from canary clearly: a canary serves real responses to a slice of users and so carries real risk, whereas a shadow serves no responses and carries essentially no user risk, which makes shadowing the safer first step before I ever promote a version to a canary.
